paragraphs.heading: What longshore drift is
paragraphs.text: Longshore drift is the movement of sediment along a coast, running parallel to the shore. The material can be clay, silt, sand, pebbles, shingle or shells. It is carried by a longshore current, and the drift is simply the sediment that this current moves. Both the current and the moving sediment stay within the surf zone. Another name for the process is littoral drift.

paragraphs.heading: It all depends on the angle
paragraphs.text: The angle at which waves arrive decides how the drift behaves. When wind comes in at a slant, it pushes water sideways along the coast and sets up a current that runs parallel to the shore. Scientists came to see the angle of wave approach as crucial for moving sediment, and longshore currents as the main force carrying it along the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Sand that zigzags
paragraphs.text: Sand on the beach itself also moves on these slanting-wind days. A breaking wave runs up the beach at an angle, which is called the swash, and gravity then drains the water straight back down the slope, at right angles to the shore, which is called the backwash. The result is a sawtooth path, and sand can travel along the beach many tens of meters in a day. This is called beach drift, though some researchers count it as part of longshore drift, since the overall effect is sand moving along the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Sand beaches and shingle beaches
paragraphs.text: Drift works a little differently depending on the size of the sediment, so a sandy beach and a shingle beach do not behave the same way. Sand is moved mostly by the back-and-forth push of breaking waves, by the impact of those waves, and by the drag of the longshore current on the bed. Shingle beaches are much steeper, so plunging breakers are more likely there. Without a wide surf zone, most of the movement on a shingle beach happens in the swash zone.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea developed
paragraphs.text: People knew in ancient times that coasts erode and sediment moves, especially where shores change dramatically, but those early accounts were mostly anecdotal. Fishermen, sailors and locals saw sand and gravel apparently travelling down beaches without understanding why. Systematic study began in the mid-1800s, with early theories from the French engineer Jean-Baptiste Fourier and the Irish geologist Robert Mallet. They studied waves and sediment before the term longshore drift had even been coined. In the early 20th century, oceanographers and coastal engineers sharpened the explanation a great deal.

paragraphs.heading: Beaches shaped by drift
paragraphs.text: One idea from that period was the drift-aligned beach: a beach shaped by the prevailing wind and wave directions, with sand building up at one side and wearing away at the other. Sand moved by drift can also be stored for a while. Ebb-tidal shoals at inlets hold sand delivered by longshore transport and can pass it on to other beaches. That makes them both sources and sinks in a coast's sediment budget.
